title: How Oil Made the US Dollar the World's Money

segments.text: Right now, almost every barrel of oil on Earth is priced in one currency. Not the currency of the country that pumps it. Not the currency of the country that buys it. The U.S. dollar. And that one fact lets America borrow cheaper than almost anyone, cut whole countries off from the world economy, and spend money other nations simply can't. But here's the strange part. It was never written into a treaty. It began with a broken promise, an oil embargo, and a secret deal in the desert. And in 2024, millions of people believed that deal had just expired. So what really happened?

To understand it, we have to go back to July 1944. The Second World War is still raging, but delegates from 44 Allied nations gather at a hotel in the mountains of New Hampshire, in a small town called Bretton Woods. Their job is to design the money system for the world after the war. And America walks in holding almost every card. Its factories are untouched. Europe is in ruins. And the United States holds roughly two-thirds of all the gold in the world's central banks.

So the system they build puts the dollar at the center of everything. The dollar is fixed to gold, at 35 dollars an ounce. The British pound, the French franc, the German mark and the Japanese yen are all fixed to the dollar. And if a foreign central bank holds dollars, it can hand them back to America and get gold in return. The dollar becomes as good as gold. For about twenty years, it works.

Then, in the 1960s, the cracks appear. America is spending heavily, on the war in Vietnam and on huge programs at home. It creates far more dollars than it has gold to back them. Those dollars pile up in banks across Europe, and some governments start to get nervous. France, under President Charles de Gaulle, begins trading its dollars for American gold, and shipping that gold home. Others quietly follow. Between the late 1950s and 1971, America's gold reserves fall by more than half. France's finance minister, Valery Giscard d'Estaing, had a name for what America enjoyed: an exorbitant privilege. The power to pay for almost anything in a currency that only America can print.

By the summer of 1971, there are far more dollars abroad than gold left to cover them. So on the evening of August 15th, President Richard Nixon goes on live television and announces that foreign governments can no longer swap their dollars for gold. He calls it temporary. It never comes back. Overnight, the world's main currency is backed by nothing but trust in the United States. They call it the Nixon Shock. And it raises a dangerous question. If the dollar isn't tied to gold anymore, why should the world keep holding it?

Two years later, the answer arrives from the Middle East. In October 1973, Egypt and Syria launch a surprise attack on Israel. When America rushes weapons to Israel, the Arab oil producers strike back with the most powerful weapon they have. They cut production, and they embargo oil shipments to the United States. Within three months, the price of a barrel jumps from about 3 dollars to nearly 12. Americans wait for hours in lines at gas stations. Pumps run dry. The government cuts the national speed limit to 55 miles an hour, and even keeps the clocks on daylight saving time through the winter, just to save fuel. And Washington learns just how much power now sits on the other side of the world.

So Washington makes a calculation. If it can't control the oil, it can try to control the money the oil produces. In July 1974, the new Treasury Secretary, William Simon, flies to Saudi Arabia, the most powerful oil producer in the region. What comes out of those meetings shapes the next fifty years. Saudi Arabia keeps selling its oil in dollars, and backs dollar pricing across OPEC. It takes the flood of dollars it earns and invests a huge share of them back into America, buying U.S. government debt. In return, America offers weapons, investment, and security cooperation with the kingdom.

The most sensitive part, the Saudi purchases of American debt, was kept quiet. For more than four decades, the Treasury hid exactly how much Saudi Arabia held, by lumping it together with other oil exporters. The number only came out in 2016, after a news investigation and a records request. By then, the kingdom held over 116 billion dollars of U.S. government debt.

Here's why that matters so much. Think about any country that needs oil. Japan. India. Germany. Kenya. To buy it, they first need dollars. Even when two countries that aren't America trade oil with each other, the price is usually set in dollars. So they sell goods to America, borrow in dollars, or keep huge piles of dollars in reserve, just in case. Meanwhile, the oil sellers send their dollars back into American banks and American bonds. Money flows out of America to pay for oil, and flows right back in. Economists call it petrodollar recycling. And for America, it's an incredible deal. Constant demand for its currency means it can borrow more cheaply, and run deficits that would sink almost any other country.

But the loop had a dark side. In the 1970s, Western banks were overflowing with petrodollars, and they lent them out, much of it to Latin America. Then, starting in 1979, the U.S. Federal Reserve pushed interest rates sharply higher to crush inflation. At one point they hit around 20 percent. Loans in dollars suddenly became crushing. In August 1982, Mexico announced it could no longer pay. Country after country followed, and Latin America fell into what became known as the lost decade.

Fast forward to today, and the dollar is still the king of world money. It makes up close to 60 percent of the world's foreign currency reserves, and it's on one side of nearly 9 in every 10 currency trades. That's what gives American sanctions their bite. Cut a country off from dollars, and you cut it off from most of the world economy. Just ask Iran. Or Russia, which in 2022 saw roughly 300 billion dollars of its central bank reserves frozen almost overnight. And when the dollar gets stronger, every poorer country that borrowed in dollars suddenly owes more, without borrowing a single extra cent.

Which brings us to June 2024. A story exploded across social media. The fifty-year petrodollar agreement between America and Saudi Arabia had just expired, and the dollar's reign was over. Millions of people shared it. There was just one problem. There was no fifty-year contract to expire. The 1974 arrangement was never a treaty with an end date. It was a set of understandings, some of them secret, held together by shared interests. And that's actually more important than any contract. Because if the petrodollar runs on interests, not paper, then the real question is: what happens when those interests change?

And they are changing. America is now the biggest oil producer in history, and buys far less oil from the Gulf than it used to. Saudi Arabia's biggest customer today is China. In 2023, it was Beijing, not Washington, that brokered a deal restoring ties between Saudi Arabia and its old rival, Iran. In 2024, Saudi Arabia's central bank joined mBridge, a project that lets central banks settle payments directly in their own digital currencies, without touching the dollar. Beijing has been pushing to pay for more of its energy in its own currency, the yuan. And countries from Russia to India have settled some oil trades in currencies other than the dollar. The dollar's share of global reserves has slipped from about 71 percent in the year 2000, to under 60 percent today.

But here's the catch. Leaving the dollar is much harder than talking about it. To replace it, a currency needs huge, open markets, money that can move freely across borders, and courts that investors trust. China still tightly controls money moving in and out of the country. The euro has no single government standing behind it. Most of the world's trade deals, loans and savings are still written in dollars, and unwinding all of that would take decades. So for now, the world keeps running on dollars. Not because everyone loves the dollar, but because nothing else is ready.

And that's why central banks are quietly hedging their bets, by buying gold at the fastest pace in decades. More than a thousand tonnes a year, three years in a row. The same metal the dollar was cut loose from in 1971. In the next video, we follow that gold. Who's buying it, where it's going, and what they're preparing for.
